summaries.example: Imagine saying, “The golden mountain is golden.” Findlay used this strange example to ask whether we can talk truthfully about something that does not exist. One philosopher, Russell, said no. Findlay defended the idea that we can think about imagined or possible things without claiming they are real.
summaries.summary: John Niemeyer Findlay was a twentieth-century philosopher from South Africa who taught in several countries. He studied many different parts of philosophy. He wrote about objects, the mind, ethics, language, time, art, and the nature of reality. Findlay supported realism, the view that the world is not simply made by our minds. He also defended the thought that people can think about nonexistent or possible objects. This led him to discuss examples such as golden mountains and wishes for things that are not yet real. Findlay believed that mental life is usually directed toward objects or situations, even when those objects are imagined. He translated Husserl's Logical Investigations and admired Husserl's careful study of experience, although he rejected Husserl's move toward idealism. Findlay's work on past, present, and future helped inspire tense logic. His later Gifford Lectures presented a large, mystical picture of reality, influenced by Plato, Plotinus, and Hindu and Buddhist sources. He also criticized Wittgenstein's views about language and inner experience. The entry presents Findlay as a wide-ranging thinker who often challenged the main direction of twentieth-century philosophy.
key_ideas: Findlay was a philosopher who worked on language, time, the mind, values, and reality.
He defended older European philosophers such as Brentano, Meinong, and Husserl while also engaging with Russell and Wittgenstein.
He helped develop the study of tense logic, which examines how statements change when we talk about past, present, and future.
He believed that thoughts can reach beyond actual objects to imagined, possible, or incomplete things.
His later philosophy explored an ideal reality influenced by Plato, Plotinus, and Hindu and Buddhist writings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Findlay shows that philosophy can connect many subjects. Questions about time affect logic, while questions about wishes and values connect the mind to ethics. His disagreements with Russell, Husserl, and Wittgenstein also show that philosophers can respect an important thinker while rejecting some of that thinker's ideas. Studying Findlay helps us see that there can be more than one serious way to understand language, thought, and reality.

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “The present king of France is bald.” Russell treated such sentences by analyzing whether any person has the relevant properties; this avoids treating a nonexistent king as an object. Findlay thought this strategy missed something about thought and desire. Someone wishing for a philosopher's stone is not merely wishing that an existing object acquire certain properties. The wish is directed toward a possible object beyond the actual world. This illustrates Findlay's defense of Meinong's view that objects need not exist in order to be objects of thought or to possess describable characteristics.
summaries.summary: John Niemeyer Findlay was a South African philosopher whose career moved among several philosophical traditions. He defended realism and developed sustained interpretations of Meinong, Brentano, Husserl, Hegel, Plato, Plotinus, and Wittgenstein. His work therefore cannot be reduced to either analytic philosophy or phenomenology. Findlay's book on Meinong defended a distinction between existence and the status of objects that can be thought about, described, or situated in possible domains. Against Russell's criticism, Findlay held that nonexistent objects may be subjects of predication without thereby existing. This distinction supported his later account of intentionality in Values and Intentions. Mental acts are directed toward objects, but their presentation can be clear or obscure, complete or partial, and concentrated or spread through behavior. Findlay also connected mental intentionality with ethics. Wishes aim at changing what is the case, and reflection can move from concern for one's own good toward more general concern for other persons and impersonal values. His phenomenology of mind remained in tension with his treatment of bodily feeling and with his realism about the physical world. Findlay admired Husserl's analytical work and translated the Logical Investigations, but rejected Husserlian idealism and defended the independent reality of the natural world. In the philosophy of time, Findlay proposed a modal treatment of tense and helped inspire later tense logic. He argued that a timeless, date-based description does not by itself explain change or why the past leaves traces available in the present while the future does not. key_ideas: Findlay worked across analytic philosophy, phenomenology, ethics, philosophy of mind, aesthetics, and metaphysics rather than staying within one school.
In defending Meinong, he distinguished existence from being a possible or describable object of thought; he argued that this distinction helps explain wishes, fiction, and incomplete possibilities.
He treated intentionality as central to mental life, but also acknowledged difficulties involving pain and other experiences that do not seem straightforwardly directed at objects.
His account of ethics began with wishes for changes in the world and developed toward impersonal value, fairness, freedom, and concern for other persons.
Findlay resisted Husserl's idealism while valuing Husserl's analyses of meaning, experience, and inner time-consciousness.

His account of tense logic treated tense as more than an omitted date. He argued that tensed statements express temporal modes and that a dated, static picture of the universe leaves out important features of time, including our evidence for the past but not the future.
summaries.why_it_matters: Findlay is important because he connects debates that are often taught separately. His discussion of nonexistent objects bears on fiction, imagination, and reference. His account of intentionality links philosophy of mind to moral reasoning. His treatment of tense helped shape a major area of philosophical logic, while his metaphysics asks whether contradictions in ordinary experience reveal limits in our concepts or clues to a deeper order. The entry also illustrates how philosophical progress can involve disagreement between traditions rather than simple replacement of one tradition by another.

important_terms.definition: The view that reality exists independently of being produced by human thought or language; Findlay used it against forms of idealism.
The philosophical study of what kinds of entities there are and how they are related.
The directedness of mental states toward an object, content, state of affairs, or possibility.
The philosophical description of structures of conscious experience, associated in Findlay's work especially with Husserl.
A logical study of the inferential behavior of statements marked as past, present, or future.
A theory of value concerned with goodness, badness, obligation, and related evaluative concepts.
A philosophical method in which tensions or contradictions are used to develop or transform a position.
A philosophical view associated with Plato and Plotinus that gives central importance to intelligible realities and an ultimate principle.

summaries.example: Suppose your class is planning a play about a dragon that never existed. You can still say, “The dragon is enormous,” and everyone can understand which imagined creature you mean. Findlay's discussion of Meinong asks whether this means the dragon is an object of thought without being a real animal. Russell would try to avoid talking as if the dragon existed. Findlay thought that approach might leave out something important about imagination and about wishes for things that are not currently real.
summaries.summary: John Niemeyer Findlay was a twentieth-century philosopher who was born in South Africa and taught in universities across several countries. His interests crossed the usual boundaries between philosophical subjects. He studied Meinong's theory of objects, the mind and values, Husserl's phenomenology, time and tense, aesthetics, Hegel, Plato, Plotinus, and Wittgenstein. Findlay often stood between competing traditions. He defended realism, yet he also explored mystical and ideal forms of metaphysics. He used phenomenological description to study how things appear in experience, while also engaging in the careful arguments associated with analytic philosophy. A central issue in his work was intentionality: thoughts and wishes are normally directed toward something. In defending Meinong, Findlay argued that imagined, impossible, or nonexistent objects can still be discussed and can have properties in descriptions, without being ordinary existing things. This helped him explain why a wish for something not yet real is not simply a wish that an existing object change. In ethics, Findlay argued that reflection can broaden concern from one's own interests to the interests of others and to values such as fairness and freedom. Findlay praised Husserl's analyses of meaning and experience, especially his work on time, but rejected Husserl's idealist conclusions and maintained that the natural world is not merely mind-made. He is also associated with the beginnings of tense logic, which studies the reasoning patterns of tensed statements. Findlay distinguished tense from simply adding dates and argued that a date-based picture may fail to explain change and our special knowledge of the past. key_ideas: Findlay was a broad-ranging philosopher who wrote about language, the mind, ethics, logic, art, and reality.
He defended Meinong's idea that something can be an object of thought without existing in the ordinary physical world.
He argued that most mental activity is directed toward something, but he also examined difficult cases such as pain and bodily feelings.
Findlay connected ethics with the way people move from personal concerns toward more general concern for others.
He admired Husserl's careful descriptions of experience but rejected the view that reality is mainly made by the mind.
His work on tense logic helped philosophers study how past, present, and future statements work. He also argued that time involves change, not just a collection of dates.
summaries.why_it_matters: Findlay's work matters because it shows how one philosopher can bring together logic, psychology, ethics, and metaphysics. His arguments about imagined objects raise questions about stories, dreams, and possibilities. His ideas about tense help explain why “it happened” is not exactly the same as “it happens at a certain date.” His debates with Husserl, Russell, and Wittgenstein also teach us that philosophy develops through careful comparison of different ways to understand the world.

important_terms.definition: The study of what is real and what kinds of things can exist or be talked about.
The view that the world is not simply created by our minds or language.
The fact that a thought, wish, or feeling is about something.
A study of conscious experience, including how things appear to us.

The study of values, including goodness, fairness, and what people ought to do.
A pattern of reasoning that uses tensions or opposing ideas to reach a broader understanding.
